topics.title: Photosynthesis: why it matters and simple experiments

learn.hook: Every grain of rice, every roti and every breath of oxygen you take traces back to a green leaf trapping sunlight.
points: Photosynthesis is a physico-chemical process by which green plants use light energy to synthesise organic compounds.
It is the primary source of all food on Earth and is responsible for the release of oxygen into the atmosphere.
Variegated leaf experiment: a leaf with green and non-green patches, kept in light and tested for starch, shows starch only in green parts, so chlorophyll is needed.
Half-covered leaf experiment: a leaf partly covered with black paper and kept in light shows starch only in the exposed part, so light is needed.
KOH half-leaf experiment: part of a leaf is enclosed in a tube with KOH-soaked cotton (KOH absorbs CO₂); only the part exposed to air tests positive for starch, so CO₂ is needed.

example.q: In the KOH half-leaf experiment, why does the enclosed half give a negative starch test?
steps: KOH absorbs CO₂ from the air in the tube.
Without CO₂, that part cannot photosynthesise.
No photosynthesis means no starch.
example.answer: KOH removes CO₂, so no photosynthesis and no starch.

learn.reallife: In school labs, the starch test uses iodine solution, and boiling the leaf in alcohol must be done in a water bath, never over a direct flame, because alcohol catches fire easily.

topics.title: Early experiments: from Priestley to van Niel

learn.hook: A candle, a mouse, a mint plant and a glass jar: Joseph Priestley's 1770s experiments launched our understanding of photosynthesis.
points: Joseph Priestley (1770s): a candle in a closed bell jar went out and a mouse suffocated; with a mint plant inside, the candle kept burning and the mouse lived. He hypothesised that plants restore to the air what breathing animals and burning candles remove. He discovered oxygen in 1774.

Jan Ingenhousz: sunlight is essential for the plant to purify the air; an aquatic plant formed bubbles (later shown to be oxygen) around its green parts in bright sunlight, not in the dark. So only green parts release oxygen.
Julius von Sachs (1854): glucose is made in the green parts of plants and is usually stored as starch; chlorophyll is located in special bodies later called chloroplasts.

T.W. Engelmann: split light with a prism and lit the green alga Cladophora placed in a suspension of aerobic bacteria. Bacteria gathered mainly in blue and red light, giving the first action spectrum of photosynthesis.

Cornelius van Niel, studying purple and green bacteria: photosynthesis is a light-dependent reaction where hydrogen from an oxidisable compound reduces CO₂ (2H₂A + CO₂ → 2A + CH₂O + H₂O). With H₂S, sulphur bacteria give sulphur, not O₂, so in green plants O₂ comes from water. Correct equation: 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6H₂O + 6O₂ (in light).

example.q: Using the equation 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6H₂O + 6O₂, how many oxygen atoms in the O₂ released come from water?
steps: 6O₂ contains 12 oxygen atoms.
van Niel showed all released O₂ comes from water.
12 H₂O supply exactly 12 oxygen atoms.
example.answer: All 12 oxygen atoms come from water.

learn.reallife: Engelmann's bacteria trick is similar to how scientists now use oxygen sensors to measure photosynthesis of crops in ICAR field trials.

learn.hook: The 'dark reaction' doesn't happen in the dark. That's one of the most misunderstood names in biology.
points: Photosynthesis occurs mainly in green leaves, but also in other green parts. Mesophyll cells have many chloroplasts.
Chloroplasts usually align along the walls of mesophyll cells so they receive optimum incident light.
Inside the chloroplast there is a division of labour. The membrane system (grana and stroma lamellae) traps light energy and makes ATP and NADPH: the light reactions (photochemical reactions).

In the stroma, enzymatic reactions synthesise sugar, which forms starch. These are not directly light-driven but depend on ATP and NADPH from the light reactions, so by convention they are called dark reactions (carbon reactions).
The term 'dark reaction' does not mean they occur in darkness or that they do not depend on light.

example.q: Why does sugar synthesis in the stroma stop soon after the light is switched off?
steps: Sugar synthesis needs ATP and NADPH.
These are made only by the light reactions in the thylakoid membranes.
Once light stops, ATP and NADPH run out, and the carbon reactions stop.
example.answer: Because the dark reactions depend on ATP and NADPH from the light reactions.

learn.reallife: Paddy farmers in Punjab know rice plants grow best in full sun; shaded rice gives poorer yield because the light reactions slow down.

learn.hook: Leaves look green because chlorophyll reflects green light. The colours it actually uses are blue and red.
points: Paper chromatography of leaf pigments separates four pigments: chlorophyll a (bright or blue-green), chlorophyll b (yellow-green), xanthophylls (yellow) and carotenoids (yellow to yellow-orange).
Pigments absorb light at specific wavelengths. A graph of absorption at different wavelengths is the absorption spectrum; chlorophyll a absorbs most in the blue and red regions.

A graph of the rate of photosynthesis at different wavelengths is the action spectrum. It correlates closely with the absorption spectrum: most photosynthesis occurs in blue and red light, though some occurs at other wavelengths.
Chlorophyll a is the chief pigment of photosynthesis.

Accessory pigments (chlorophyll b, xanthophylls, carotenoids) absorb light and transfer energy to chlorophyll a. They widen the range of wavelengths used and protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation.

example.q: A student runs a chromatogram of spinach pigments. Name the four bands and their colours.
steps: Chlorophyll a: bright or blue-green.
Chlorophyll b: yellow-green.
Xanthophylls: yellow.
Carotenoids: yellow to yellow-orange.
example.answer: Chlorophyll a (blue-green), chlorophyll b (yellow-green), xanthophylls (yellow), carotenoids (yellow-orange).

learn.reallife: Autumn leaves of Kashmir's chinar trees turn golden as chlorophyll breaks down and the yellow-orange carotenoids, hidden until then, show through.

topics.title: Light reaction: photosystems, Z scheme and splitting of water

learn.hook: Photosystem II comes first in the chain but was discovered second. Its name is a history lesson, not a sequence.
points: The light reactions (photochemical phase) include light absorption, water splitting, oxygen release and formation of ATP and NADPH.

Pigments form light harvesting complexes (LHC) in Photosystem I (PS I) and Photosystem II (PS II), named in the order of discovery, not function. Each LHC has hundreds of pigment molecules bound to proteins forming the antennae; a single chlorophyll a molecule is the reaction centre.
The PS I reaction centre absorbs maximally at 700 nm (P700); the PS II reaction centre at 680 nm (P680).

Z scheme: PS II absorbs 680 nm light, electrons are excited and accepted by an acceptor, then pass downhill through an electron transport chain (cytochromes) to PS I. PS I electrons, excited by 700 nm light, go to another acceptor and then downhill to NADP⁺, reducing it to NADPH + H⁺.
Water splitting, associated with PS II on the inner side of the thylakoid membrane, replaces the electrons lost by PS II: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + O₂ + 4e⁻. Protons and O₂ are released into the thylakoid lumen.

example.q: How many molecules of water must be split to release 3 molecules of O₂?
steps: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + O₂ + 4e⁻: 2 water molecules give 1 O₂.
For 3 O₂: 3 × 2 = 6 water molecules.

learn.reallife: The oxygen in the air over India's forests, from the Sundarbans to the Western Ghats, is released by this water-splitting reaction.

learn.hook: ATP synthase is a real molecular turbine: protons rush through it like water through a dam at Bhakra-Nangal, and that flow makes ATP.
points: Photophosphorylation is the synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate in the presence of light.
Non-cyclic photophosphorylation: PS II and PS I work in series, connected by the electron transport chain; both ATP and NADPH + H⁺ are made.

Cyclic photophosphorylation: only PS I works; electrons cycle back to PS I through the electron transport chain. It occurs in stroma lamellae, which lack PS II and NADP reductase. Only ATP is made, not NADPH. It also occurs when only light beyond 680 nm is available.

Chemiosmotic hypothesis: ATP synthesis is linked to a proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane. Protons build up in the lumen because (a) water is split on the inner side, (b) a carrier moves protons from the stroma into the lumen as electrons are transported, and (c) NADP reductase on the stroma side removes protons from the stroma. The lumen pH falls.

ATP synthase has two parts: F₀ (CF₀), a transmembrane channel for facilitated diffusion of protons, and F₁ (CF₁), protruding into the stroma. Protons flowing back through F₀ cause a conformational change in F₁ that makes ATP. Chemiosmosis needs a membrane, a proton pump, a proton gradient and ATP synthase.

example.q: Give two differences between cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation.
steps: Cyclic: only PS I; non-cyclic: PS II and PS I.
Cyclic makes only ATP; non-cyclic makes ATP and NADPH.
Cyclic occurs in stroma lamellae; non-cyclic in grana.
example.answer: Cyclic uses only PS I and makes only ATP (stroma lamellae); non-cyclic uses both photosystems and makes ATP and NADPH (grana).

learn.reallife: Hydroelectric dams such as Bhakra-Nangal turn falling water into electricity; ATP synthase turns falling protons into ATP.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does light actually make ATP?' Explain photophosphorylation and chemiosmosis!
teach.praise: Chirp! Protons pile up in the lumen and rush through ATP synthase. Light becomes ATP!
teach.nudge: Good! What is the difference between cyclic and non-cyclic, and what drives ATP synthase?

learn.hook: Melvin Calvin fed radioactive ¹⁴CO₂ to algae and traced where the carbon went. The first stop was a 3-carbon acid, and a Nobel Prize followed.
points: ATP and NADPH from the light reactions, with CO₂, are used in the biosynthetic phase to make sugars. O₂ diffuses out. Synthesis continues briefly after light stops, then halts.

Melvin Calvin used radioactive ¹⁴C in algal photosynthesis and found the first CO₂ fixation product is a 3-carbon acid, 3-phosphoglyceric acid (PGA): the C3 pathway. In some plants the first product is oxaloacetic acid (OAA), a 4-carbon acid: the C4 pathway.
In C3 plants the primary CO₂ acceptor is ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP), a 5-carbon ketose sugar.

The Calvin cycle occurs in all photosynthetic plants and has three stages: carboxylation (RuBisCO fixes CO₂ with RuBP to give two molecules of 3-PGA), reduction (2 ATP and 2 NADPH per CO₂ fixed, leading to carbohydrate), and regeneration of RuBP (1 ATP per CO₂).
So each CO₂ needs 3 ATP and 2 NADPH. One glucose needs 6 CO₂ and 6 turns: 18 ATP and 12 NADPH. The extra ATP need may be met by cyclic photophosphorylation.

example.q: How much ATP and NADPH are needed to make 2 molecules of glucose by the Calvin cycle?
steps: One glucose: 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.
Two glucose: 2 × 18 = 36 ATP and 2 × 12 = 24 NADPH.

learn.reallife: Most Indian staples, including rice and wheat, are C3 plants that fix carbon directly through the Calvin cycle.

quiz.q: The primary CO₂ acceptor in C3 plants is:
quiz.explain: Ribulose bisphosphate, a 5-carbon sugar, accepts CO₂.

quiz.q: The first stable product of CO₂ fixation in C3 plants is:
quiz.explain: Calvin found the 3-carbon PGA first.

quiz.q: How many ATP molecules are needed to fix one molecule of CO₂ in the Calvin cycle?
quiz.explain: 2 ATP for reduction + 1 ATP for regeneration = 3.

quiz.q: How many turns of the Calvin cycle produce one molecule of glucose?
quiz.explain: Six CO₂, one per turn, make one glucose.

quiz.q: How many NADPH molecules are needed to make one glucose molecule?

6 CO₂ per glucose

quiz.q: Which enzyme catalyses carboxylation of RuBP?
quiz.explain: RuBP carboxylase-oxygenase fixes CO₂.

quiz.explain: ¹⁴C labelling revealed PGA as the first product.

teach.praise: Tweet! Carboxylation, reduction, regeneration. 18 ATP and 12 NADPH per glucose. Sweet maths!

topics.title: The C4 pathway (Hatch and Slack pathway)

learn.hook: Maize, sorghum and sugarcane thrive in hot Indian summers with super yields. Their leaves have a 'wreath' of special cells that act like CO₂ pumps.
points: C4 plants are adapted to dry tropical regions (e.g. maize, sorghum). Their first CO₂ fixation product is the 4-carbon OAA, but they still use the Calvin cycle as the main biosynthetic pathway. They tolerate higher temperatures, respond to high light, lack photorespiration and have greater biomass productivity.
Kranz anatomy ('Kranz' = wreath): large bundle sheath cells around vascular bundles, with many chloroplasts, thick walls impervious to gas exchange and no intercellular spaces.

In mesophyll cells, the primary CO₂ acceptor is the 3-carbon phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP), fixed by PEP carboxylase (PEPcase) to OAA. OAA forms other 4-carbon acids such as malic acid or aspartic acid, which move to the bundle sheath cells.

In bundle sheath cells, the C4 acids are broken down to release CO₂ and a 3-carbon molecule. The CO₂ enters the Calvin cycle; the 3-carbon molecule returns to the mesophyll and is converted back to PEP, completing the cycle.
Mesophyll cells lack RuBisCO; bundle sheath cells are rich in RuBisCO but lack PEPcase.

example.q: Trace one carbon from atmospheric CO₂ to sugar in a maize leaf.
steps: In mesophyll, PEPcase fixes CO₂ with PEP to form OAA.
OAA becomes malate or aspartate and moves to the bundle sheath.
There it is decarboxylated, releasing CO₂.
RuBisCO fixes this CO₂ in the Calvin cycle to make sugar.
example.answer: Mesophyll (PEP → OAA → malate) → bundle sheath (CO₂ released) → Calvin cycle

learn.reallife: Sugarcane in Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra and maize in Karnataka are C4 crops that give high yields in hot, sunny conditions.

teach.ask: Gappu wonders why maize and sugarcane grow so well in hot summers. Explain the C4 pathway and Kranz anatomy!
teach.praise: Chirp! PEP grabs CO₂ in mesophyll and delivers it to RuBisCO in the bundle sheath. Super crop!
teach.nudge: Good! What fixes CO₂ first in C4 plants, and where does the Calvin cycle happen?

learn.hook: The world's most abundant enzyme sometimes grabs the wrong gas. When RuBisCO binds O₂ instead of CO₂, the plant wastes energy.
points: RuBisCO, the most abundant enzyme in the world, has an active site that can bind both CO₂ and O₂. It has a much greater affinity for CO₂, but the relative concentrations of O₂ and CO₂ decide which binds.
In C3 plants some O₂ binds RuBisCO, reducing CO₂ fixation. RuBP then combines with O₂ to form one molecule of PGA and one of phosphoglycolate: photorespiration.
Photorespiration makes no sugar, no ATP and no NADPH; instead CO₂ is released and ATP is used. So it is a wasteful process.

C4 plants do not show photorespiration: breaking down C4 acids in bundle sheath cells raises the CO₂ concentration around RuBisCO, so it acts as a carboxylase and its oxygenase activity is minimised. This is one reason C4 plants have higher productivity and tolerate higher temperatures.

C3 vs C4: primary acceptor RuBP (5C) vs PEP (3C); first product PGA (3C) vs OAA (4C); fixing enzyme RuBisCO vs PEPcase (then RuBisCO); Kranz anatomy absent vs present; photorespiration present vs negligible; Calvin cycle in mesophyll vs bundle sheath.

steps: RuBisCO binds O₂ instead of CO₂, forming PGA and phosphoglycolate.
No sugar, ATP or NADPH is made.
CO₂ that was fixed is released and ATP is consumed.
example.answer: Because it uses energy and releases CO₂ without making sugar, ATP or NADPH.

learn.reallife: Scientists in India and abroad are trying to engineer rice (a C3 plant) to work more like a C4 plant to cut photorespiration and raise yields.

learn.hook: Greenhouse tomato growers pump extra CO₂ into their glasshouses. Why would anyone add a 'pollutant' to plants on purpose?
points: Internal (plant) factors: number, size, age and orientation of leaves, mesophyll cells and chloroplasts, internal CO₂ and amount of chlorophyll. External factors: light, CO₂, temperature and water.

Blackman's law of limiting factors (1905): if a chemical process is affected by more than one factor, its rate is determined by the factor nearest to its minimal value. E.g. a leaf with optimal light and CO₂ may not photosynthesise if the temperature is very low.

Light: rate rises linearly with light at low intensities, then levels off; light saturation occurs at about 10% of full sunlight, so light is rarely limiting except in shade. Excess light breaks down chlorophyll and reduces photosynthesis.

CO₂: the major limiting factor (only about 0.03 to 0.04% in air). Up to about 0.05% it increases fixation; higher levels can be damaging over long periods. C4 plants saturate at about 360 µL L⁻¹; C3 plants respond up to beyond 450 µL L⁻¹, so present CO₂ levels limit C3 plants. Greenhouse tomatoes and bell peppers grown in CO₂-enriched air give higher yields.

Temperature: dark reactions are enzymatic and temperature-controlled; light reactions are much less affected. C4 plants have higher temperature optima than C3; tropical plants have higher optima than temperate ones. Water acts indirectly: water stress closes stomata (less CO₂) and makes leaves wilt (less surface area and activity).

example.q: A C3 plant under bright light shows no increase in photosynthesis when light is doubled, but a large increase when CO₂ is raised. What is the limiting factor?
steps: Increasing light has no effect, so light is not limiting.
Increasing CO₂ raises the rate, so CO₂ is nearest its minimum.
By Blackman's law, CO₂ is the limiting factor.

learn.reallife: Polyhouse farmers in Maharashtra and Karnataka grow capsicum and tomatoes under controlled conditions; CO₂ enrichment and shade nets help manage limiting factors.

quiz.q: Blackman's law of limiting factors was given in:

quiz.q: According to Blackman's law, the rate of a process is determined by the factor:

quiz.q: Light saturation for photosynthesis occurs at about what percentage of full sunlight?

quiz.explain: C3 plants are limited by current CO₂ levels.
options: They are C3 plants that respond to higher CO₂ with faster photosynthesis
They are C4 plants that need no CO₂

quiz.q: Water stress reduces photosynthesis mainly by:
quiz.explain: Closed stomata cut CO₂ entry and wilted leaves have less area.
quiz.mistake: Thinks water acts mainly as a reactant

quiz.q: C4 plants show CO₂ saturation at about:
quiz.explain: C4 saturate at about 360; C3 only beyond 450.

quiz.q: Which reactions of photosynthesis are more strongly controlled by temperature?
quiz.explain: Enzymatic carbon reactions are temperature-sensitive.
